take: The Hormuz disruption has escalated from rhetoric to physical strikes on tankers, with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards hitting the Togo-flagged product tanker Trend and Macron now calling a G7 emergency release as Europe loses Saudi crude deliveries and diesel cracks push deeper into record territory. The freight transmission is already violent: the Baltic’s Middle East Gulf–China VLCC benchmark broke the equivalent of $1m a day for the first time, and Maersk’s confirmed 26-ship order for 18,000 teu units signals carriers are positioning for structurally longer routings rather than a temporary spike. Positioning-wise, the tell is in the paper market rather than the physical — with US crude forecast at a record 13.8m b/d in 2026 and US LNG exports up 23% year-on-year to 17.4 Bcf/d, the upside is being priced into freight and distillate cracks rather than flat price, whilst emergency stock releases would flatten the curve without fixing the tonne-mile problem. The cross-market link to watch is gasoil versus bunker: European LNG spot prices up 150% are pulling gas into power and away from industrial demand, whilst a $700/t carbon price is what GCMD and BCG reckon is needed before methanol or ammonia take meaningful bunker share — under the IMO’s proposed $380/t penalty, methanol-fitted ships would still burn conventional fuel almost all the time. In the next 24 hours, watch whether the G7 actually convenes on a co-ordinated release, whether the Black Sea truce draft from Turkey gains Russian and Ukrainian traction, and whether VLCC rates hold above the $1m/day print or fade on any de-escalation headline.

items.title: What goes into diesel prices?
items.summary: The price of distillate fuel oil, often sold as diesel, is driven by the price of crude oil, retail margins, distribution costs, taxes, and crack spreads, the indicator we use for refining margins. Tight global supplies of distillate fuel oil and elevated crude oil prices have driven prices higher in recent months.
